hints: Compare the physical states given in the equation for the catalyst and for hydrogen peroxide.
walkthrough:
Picture what is mixed together**
You have aqueous hydrogen peroxide, so the $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ particles are dissolved in water, plus solid $\text{MnO}_2$ powder sitting in that solution. The catalyst is not dissolved, it stays as a separate solid surface.

Link phase to type of catalysis**
When catalyst and reactants are in the same phase it is homogeneous, when they are in different phases it is heterogeneous. Here solid versus aqueous solution means different phases, so this is heterogeneous catalysis.
Final answer: Heterogeneous catalysis, as $\text{MnO}_2$ is a solid which is in a different state / phase to the aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ reactant.

hints: Start by finding a pair of experiments where only $[\text{I}^-]$ changes while $[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]$ and $[\text{H}^+]$ stay constant.
Next look for pairs where $[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]$ changes but you can allow for the change in $[\text{I}^-]$ you have already worked out.
Compare experiments 1 and 4, or 3 and 4, to see what happens to rate when $[\text{H}^+]$ is greatly increased.
Remember to combine your three orders into the form $\text{rate} = k[\text{A}]^m[\text{B}]^n$.
walkthrough:
Find the order in iodide**
Keep everything else the same. Experiments 2 and 3 are perfect because $[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2] = 0.0225$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and $[\text{H}^+] = 0.0125$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ in both. $[\text{I}^-]$ doubles from $0.0600$ to $0.120$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and the rate doubles from $2.42 \times 10^{-3}$ to $4.84 \times 10^{-3}$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}$. Doubling concentration doubles rate, so rate is directly proportional to $[\text{I}^-]$. That is first order.

Find the order in hydrogen peroxide**
Now compare experiments 1 and 2. $[\text{I}^-]$ doubles from $0.0300$ to $0.0600$, which alone would double the rate. At the same time $[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]$ halves from $0.0450$ to $0.0225$, yet the rate stays exactly the same at $2.42 \times 10^{-3}$. The halving of $[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]$ must exactly cancel the doubling effect of $[\text{I}^-]$. So halving $[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]$ halves the rate. That is also first order.

Find the order in hydrogen ions**
Compare experiments 1 and 4. $[\text{I}^-]$ goes $\times 4$ from $0.0300$ to $0.120$, which alone would make rate $\times 4$. $[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]$ is constant at $0.0450$ and $[\text{H}^+]$ goes $\times 4$ from $0.0125$ to $0.0500$. The observed rate goes $\times 4$ from $2.42 \times 10^{-3}$ to $9.68 \times 10^{-3}$. All of that $\times 4$ is already explained by $[\text{I}^-]$, so $[\text{H}^+]$ has no effect. That is zero order.

Write the rate equation**
Put the orders together, omitting the zero order reactant or writing it to power zero:
$$\text{rate} = k[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2]^1[\text{I}^-]^1[\text{H}^+]^0$$
which simplifies to:
$$\text{rate} = k[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2][\text{I}^-]$$

Final answer: From expts 2 and 3: $[	ext{I}^-]$ $	imes 2$, rate $	imes 2$, so first order in $[	ext{I}^-]$.
From expts 1 and 2: $[	ext{I}^-]$ $	imes 2$ would $	imes 2$ rate, but $[	ext{H}_2	ext{O}_2]$ $	imes 0.5$ leaves rate unchanged, so first order in $[	ext{H}_2	ext{O}_2]$.
From expts 1 and 4: $[	ext{I}^-]$ $	imes 4$ and $[	ext{H}^+]$ $	imes 4$, rate $	imes 4$, so zero order in $[	ext{H}^+]$.
$	ext{rate} = k[	ext{H}_2	ext{O}_2][	ext{I}^-]$

hints: Rearrange your rate equation to make $k$ the subject and choose the concentration values from Experiment 1.
Think how the units of rate, $\text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}$, divided by two concentration units must simplify.
walkthrough:
Substitute into the rearranged rate equation**
You know $\text{rate} = k[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2][\text{I}^-]$, so:
$$k = \frac{\text{rate}}{[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2][\text{I}^-]}$$
Using Experiment 1:
$$k = \frac{2.42 \times 10^{-3}}{0.0450 \times 0.0300}$$
$$k = \frac{2.42 \times 10^{-3}}{1.35 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.79$$

Work out the units**
Units follow the same rearrangement:
$$\text{units of } k = \frac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})(\text{mol dm}^{-3})} = \text{dm}^3 \text{mol}^{-1} \text{s}^{-1}$$
That makes sense for an overall second order reaction. So $k = 1.79$ $\text{dm}^3 \text{mol}^{-1} \text{s}^{-1}$.

hints: Pick a convenient starting concentration on the curve, for example $0.050$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, and read off the time to fall to half that value.
Then start from that half value as your new starting point and check the time needed to halve again.
walkthrough:
Read the first half-life**
Start where the curve is clearest. At $t = 0$, $[\text{CH}_3\text{N=NCH}_3] = 0.050$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Half of that is $0.025$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Slide across from $0.025$ on the y-axis to the curve and down to the time axis. You land at about $60$ s. So the first $t_{1/2} \approx 60$ s.

Read the second half-life and conclude**
Now treat $0.025$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ as your new start, at $t \approx 60$ s. Half of that is $0.0125$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Reading across and down again gives $t \approx 120$ s. The time for this second halving is $120 - 60 = 60$ s. Two successive half-lives are the same, about $60$ s, which is the fingerprint of first order kinetics.

Final answer: First $t_{1/2}$: $[\text{CH}_3\text{N=NCH}_3]$ $0.050$ to $0.025$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ takes $60$ s.\nSecond $t_{1/2}$: $0.025$ to $0.0125$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ takes $60$ s.\n$t_{1/2}$ constant at $60$ s, so first order.

hints: Recall the exact mathematical link between $k$ and $t_{1/2}$ for a first order reaction.
walkthrough:
Apply the first order half-life equation**
For first order only, half-life and $k$ are linked by a constant:
$$k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$$
Using $t_{1/2} = 60$ s:
$$k = \frac{0.693}{60} = 0.0116 \text{ s}^{-1}$$
A larger $k$ would mean a shorter half-life and a steeper curve.

hints: Think whether temperature appears in the rate equation as a concentration term or hidden inside $k$.
walkthrough:
See why k must increase**
Rate depends on concentrations and on $k$. Concentrations do not change just by heating, but particles gain kinetic energy. A greater proportion can overcome $E_a$ on collision, so the same concentrations react faster. That faster reaction at the same concentrations means the constant $k$ itself has increased, and so the overall rate increases.
Final answer: Increasing temperature increases $k$ and therefore increases the rate of reaction.
